summary: Psalm 76 begins by locating God’s known name and dwelling in Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion. It then describes God breaking weapons of war, rendering warriors and their horses powerless, and rising in judgment to save the afflicted. The psalm ends by calling people to fulfill vows and bring gifts to the one feared by earthly rulers.
whyItMatters: This chapter belongs to Book III of Psalms, where sanctuary, crisis, and God’s rule are major concerns. It presents God’s judgment as a terror to violent powers and as rescue for the afflicted.

context.author: Psalms is a collection with many writers and collections; this psalm’s heading associates it with Asaph, though the exact force of such headings is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that used Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Psalm 76 cannot be securely assigned to a single date. It belongs to a Psalter whose poems and collections developed over centuries, from the monarchy through the postexilic period.
context.setting: The poem is oriented toward Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion, with temple or sanctuary language and imagery of defeated warfare.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and worship song, with a musical heading and the performance marker Selah preserved in the text.

outline.heading: God Known in Zion
outline.note: The psalm opens with a musical heading and names Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion as places associated with God’s known name and dwelling.

outline.heading: Weapons Broken
outline.note: God breaks the weapons of war and leaves valiant soldiers, chariot, and horse unable to act.

outline.heading: Judgment from Heaven
outline.note: The psalm asks who can stand before God, then describes heaven’s judgment as the earth becomes silent and the afflicted are saved.

outline.heading: Vows and Fear
outline.note: Human wrath is restrained under God’s rule, and the surrounding peoples are summoned to fulfill vows and bring presents to the one feared by kings.

keyVerses.text: There he broke the flaming arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the weapons of war. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This line states the central image of the psalm: God disables warfare at the place associated with his dwelling.

keyVerses.text: You, even you, are to be feared. Who can stand in your sight when you are angry?
keyVerses.why: The verse turns the victory scene into direct address, stressing that God’s power demands awe.

keyVerses.text: when God arose to judgment, to save all the afflicted ones of the earth. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This explains the aim of judgment in the psalm: rescue for the afflicted, not violence for its own sake.

keyVerses.text: Make vows to Yahweh your God, and fulfill them! Let all of his neighbors bring presents to him who is to be feared.
keyVerses.why: The final movement turns the scene of judgment into a call for public response.

themes: God known in Judah and Israel
The defeat of weapons and warriors

questions.question: What does the opening heading tell us?
questions.answer: The heading says the psalm is for the Chief Musician, on stringed instruments, associated with Asaph, and called both a psalm and a song. In Psalms, headings can preserve information about performance, collection, dedication, or association, but readers differ on how much they establish about authorship or first setting.

questions.question: Where are Salem and Zion?
questions.answer: Salem is an ancient name for Jerusalem, and Zion names its holy dwelling place. The paired lines locate God’s tabernacle and dwelling in the same sacred city. The next verse places the breaking of enemy weapons there, linking the city’s protection with God’s presence.

questions.question: What is meant by God breaking the weapons of war?
questions.answer: Verse 3 says God broke the flaming arrows, shield, sword, and weapons of war. The warriors then lie plundered and unable to lift their hands, while chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep. The scene depicts military defeat and death, not merely a pause in fighting, and attributes that victory to God’s rebuke.

questions.question: What does Selah mean here?
questions.answer: Selah appears after verses 3 and 9. It is a musical or performance marker preserved in the Psalms, but its exact instruction is no longer known. Here it punctuates the scenes of broken weapons and God’s judgment on behalf of the afflicted.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say God is to be feared?
questions.answer: Fear here includes awe and terror before God’s power and judgment. The question, “Who can stand in your sight when you are angry?” follows the defeat of warriors and is answered by an earth that fears and falls silent. The setting is an overwhelming victory, not simply a calm feeling of reverence.

questions.question: Is God’s judgment presented only as destruction?
questions.answer: No. Verse 9 says God arose to judgment “to save all the afflicted ones of the earth.” The psalm does describe anger, rebuke, and defeated rulers, but it also gives judgment a protective purpose for the afflicted.

questions.question: What does “the wrath of man praises you” mean?
questions.answer: The line places human wrath within God’s victory: even hostility ends in his praise. Its second half speaks of the survivors of God’s wrath being restrained. The verse asserts that human rage cannot overturn God’s rule, but its compressed language does not spell out exactly how that reversal takes place.

questions.question: What response does the psalm ask for at the end?
questions.answer: The psalm calls people to make vows to Yahweh and fulfill them. It also tells God’s neighbors to bring presents, while the closing verse says princes and kings are subject to fear before him.

glossary.def: A figure named in the heading, likely connected with the psalm’s performance or collection use; the exact historical role is not explained in the chapter.
The musical direction in the heading, showing that the psalm was associated with accompanied performance.
A preserved performance marker in Psalms whose exact instruction is uncertain; it appears here after the breaking of weapons and after God’s saving judgment.
The word used in verse 2 for God’s dwelling in Salem; in this psalm it helps locate God’s presence with Zion.
Promises or pledged acts of worship named in verse 11; the psalm calls for them to be fulfilled.
